text: $30M FOR BIKES, ZERO BRAKES ON SPENDING. Congress wants to create a USAID-run rural mobility program, funding bicycle distribution in Sub-Saharan Africa to improve access to schools, healthcare, and jobs. The plan starts at $3M per year and ramps up to $12M annually by 2028, with no set end date. Meanwhile, USAID already funds similar programs. The agency has spent $3.5M on Bicycles for Growth, delivering bikes in Ghana, Malawi, Rwanda, Uganda, and Zambia. No comprehensive audit. No independent impact review. No clear data on how many bikes are in use. The bill requires a retroactive report on past projects—but only after the new funding is locked in. Shouldn’t we see the results first? Same idea. More money. Little accountability. @SenatorDurbin , is this about helping people—or just keeping the spending wheels turning?

text: BREAKING: Second suspect in deadly shootout with Border Patrol Agent in Vermont is charged with two felonies; Suspects had tactical gear and body armor, two-way radios By Michael Donoghue - Vermont News First Teresa Youngblut of Washington State has been identified as the second suspect in the fatal shooting of a U.S. Border Patrol Agent in Orleans County this week. Youngblut is charged with intentional use of a deadly weapon while forcibly assaulting a federal law enforcement and with discharging a firearm during an assault with deadly weapon, records show. She is named in a criminal complaint filed by the FBI and unsealed this morning in U.S. District Court in Burlington. AN 8-page affidavit outlines the case. Youngblut has been held at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, N.H. with gunshot wounds, but could be in federal court as early as this afternoon. Vermont News First initially reported the fatal shooting on Monday shortly after the 3:15 p.m. shootout. Her companion shooter, a German National, Felix Baukholt was shot dead at the scene by the Border Patrol. A search of their Prius uncovered various pieces of tactical gear, including a ballistic helmet, night-vision=goggle monocular, a tactical belt with holster and a magazine loaded with cartridges, two full-face respirators, 48 rounds of .380-caliber jacketed hollow point ammunition, a package of shooting range targets, including some were used. Also seized were two-way radios, about a dozen electronic devices and multiple removeable electronic storage devices, various identification documents, utility, lease, travel and lodging information for multiple states and a journal maintains by Youngblut. The FBI confirmed today earlier reports by Vermont News FIrst (VNF) that the two shooting suspects had been under surveillance since about Jan. 14 by Homeland Security Agents. It included monitoring the couple at the Wal-Mart in Newport from about 11:30 until 2:35 p.m. on the day of the shooting. A hotel clerk in Lyndonville reported to authorities on Jan. 14 a man and woman had checked in dressed in all-black tactical style clothing with protective equipment, the FBI said. The woman, later identified as Youngblut, was carrying an apparent firearm in an exposed carry holster, the FBI said. Investigators with Vermont State Police and Homeland Security Investigations attempted to initiate a conversation with Youngblut and Baukholt, but they declined to have an extended chat, the FBI said. The couple checked out of the motel on Jan. 14 and investigators later spotted them in similar tactical dress on Sunday Jan. 19 walking in downtown Newport with Youngblut still carrying a firearm, FBI Agent Leah Leah Bogdanowicz wrote in the criminal complaint. Youngblut was seen carrying an apparent firearm in an exposed carry holster. Vermont State Police and Homeland Security Investigations attempted to have a conversation with Youngblut and Bukholt, but they declined, the FBI said. Meanwhile the body of U.S. Border Patrol Agent David "Chris" Maland, 44, of Newport was headed from Burlington to Albany, N.Y. for a flight home to Minnesota. He was a K-9 handler with his partner Cora. He was killed in a wild shootout in Orleans County on Monday afternoon. The homicide happened during a traffic stop for a southbound car on Interstate 91 in Coventry about 9 miles south of the U.S.-Canada border. Maland was treated at the scene for a gunshot wound to the neck and was pronounced dead at North Country Hospital in Newport about 4 p.m. Baukholt was dead at the scene. Authorities have said Baukholt had overstayed his temporary work Visa. It also was unclear how he would have obtained a firearm as a non-resident. Homeland Security had been investigating the couple and a third suspect in the days leading up to the shooting. It was unknown if the Border Patrol had been briefed on the case before they were asked to pull over the vehicle. Some of the trio had been staying for several days at the Newport City Inn and Suites on East Main Street. Other reports indicate they were earlier staying in St. Johnsbury. This story will be updated throughout today.

text: BILL GATES URGES PRESIDENT RUTO TO IMPLEMENT NEW DIGITAL ID SYSTEM FOR NEWBORNS IN KENYA In a recent meeting, philanthropist and Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has urged President William Ruto of Kenya to consider the implementation of a new digital identification system for newborns in the country. This proposal aims to improve access to vital services and healthcare for all Kenyan children, enhance government record-keeping, and support overall development efforts. The New Digital ID System: Gates proposed a comprehensive digital ID system that would assign a unique identification number to every newborn in Kenya. This ID would be linked to their health records, vaccination history, and other essential information. The system would utilize secure and modern technology to ensure data privacy and security. Key Objectives: Improved Access to Healthcare: The digital ID system would make it easier for parents to access healthcare services for their newborns, including vaccinations, medical check-ups, and emergency care. text: Reimagining Nevada’s Federal Lands: Could Homesteading Work in the Silver State? Nevada and Nebraska joined the Union in 1867, but their destinies diverged sharply. Nebraska’s fertile plains welcomed homesteaders under the 1862 Homestead Act, turning federal land into private farms until just 1% remains public today. Nevada, with its rugged deserts and scant rainfall, saw little of that transformation—83% of its 70.7 million acres, or about 48 million, still sit under federal control, mostly managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). This disparity fuels a Western grievance: why do states like Nevada bear such heavy federal oversight while eastern counterparts govern their own soil? Utah’s recent lawsuit against the feds—filed in 2024 and rebuffed by the Supreme Court in January 2025—sought to reclaim 18.5 million acres of unappropriated land, spotlighting a question Nevada might soon echo: could homesteading finally unlock its vast BLM holdings? The Historical Misfire Nevada’s federal land burden isn’t a conspiracy—it’s geography. The Homestead Act offered 160 acres to anyone who’d farm it for five years, but Nevada’s 7–10 inches of annual rain and rocky soils deterred settlers. Only 2% of its land was claimed, leaving the feds in charge when statehood terms forced Nevada to “forever disclaim” unappropriated tracts. Today, the BLM stewards 41 million acres of this legacy, dwarfing Nebraska’s privatized plains. The effects ripple through Nevada’s economy and identity: limited taxable land, sluggish development approvals, and a sense of disenfranchisement as Washington, D.C., calls the shots. Yet suitability, not sentiment, determines what’s possible. Could modern homesteading—tuned to Nevada’s arid reality—recast this story? Farming: Hemp as a Desert Lifeline Traditional farming flops in Nevada’s dry expanse. Just 1% of the state (700,000 acres) grows crops, mostly alfalfa guzzling 40–50 inches of irrigated water yearly. BLM lands, often remote and parched, offer little hope for corn or wheat. Enter industrial hemp, a drought-tolerant marvel needing only 10–15 inches of water. Legal since 2018 and tested in arid states like Colorado, hemp yields 500–1,000 pounds per acre for fiber, seed, or CBD, fetching $500–$2,000 per acre versus alfalfa’s $200–$300. Nevada’s semi-arid valleys—think Elko or White Pine counties, with 8–10 inches of rain—could sustain it with modest irrigation from shallow aquifers or seasonal streams. Without hemp, viable BLM farmland tops out at 500,000–1 million acres (1.2%–2.4% of its 41 million). With it, that jumps to 2–3 million acres, supporting 6,250–18,750 homesteads of 160–320 acres each. Water remains the rub—Nevada’s over-allocated rivers and shrinking aquifers cap scale—but hemp’s thriftiness could add $1–$6 billion annually to the state’s economy, dwarfing traditional agriculture’s $300 million. It’s not Nebraska’s breadbasket, but a niche homestead revival. Ranching: Hardy Grasses to the Rescue Ranching already leans on BLM land, with 18 million acres leased for grazing at low rates—10–50 acres per animal unit month (AUM) due to sparse sagebrush and thin rains. Drought-resistant grasses like crested wheatgrass or bluebunch wheatgrass, thriving on 6–12 inches of water, could change that. Reseeding degraded BLM tracts—500,000 acres burn yearly in Nevada wildfires—boosts forage to 5–20 acres per AUM, doubling or tripling capacity. Models from Utah and Australia show sustainability with rotational grazing and solar-powered wells. Originally pegged at 15–20 million acres (36.6%–48.8% of BLM land), ranching could claim 20–25 million acres with hardy grasses, hosting 31,000–39,000 homesteads of 640 acres each (a nod to the 1916 Stock-Raising Homestead Act). This lifts grazing revenue from $150 million to $200–$300 million annually, though seeding costs ($20–$50/acre) and wild horse herds (40,000-plus in Nevada) demand upfront investment and management. It’s a rugged, viable upgrade to Nevada’s cowboy roots. Mining: The Evergreen Ace Mining needs no coaxing. Nevada leads U.S. gold production and eyes lithium for the clean-energy boom. BLM lands hold 2 million active mining acres, with exploration suggesting 5 million more (4.9%–12.2%) could fuel thousands of claims under the 1872 Mining Law. Homesteading wouldn’t reinvent this wheel—federal leases already work—but state control might speed permits. Economic stakes are sky-high: mining pumps $9 billion yearly into Nevada, untouched by hemp or grass innovations. A New Homestead Map Blend these uses, and 24–33 million BLM acres (58.5%–80.5%) could homestead: 2–3 million for hemp farming, 20–25 million for ranching, and 2–5 million for mining. The rest—8–17 million acres—stays public for conservation, recreation, or tribal needs, honoring Nevada’s ecological limits. That’s 37,250–62,750 homesteads total, a far cry from 1867’s bust. Water, infrastructure (wells, processing plants), and funding (seeding, subsidies) are hurdles, but the math holds: Nevada’s arid strengths, not its weaknesses, drive this vision. Why It Matters Nevada’s federal land lock—83% versus Nebraska’s 1%—chafes locals. The state can’t tax or fully exploit 48 million acres, stunting growth while federal rules bottleneck projects like Las Vegas sprawl. Utah’s 2024 suit, backed by Nevada and 11 other states, argued this violates state sovereignty under the Constitution’s Property Clause. The Supreme Court’s January 2025 dodge keeps the fight alive, likely headed to lower courts. Success could cede Nevada’s 41 million BLM acres to state hands, amplifying homesteading’s odds. Yet trade-offs loom. State control risks privatization—selling to developers or corporations—eroding public access cherished by hikers and hunters. Environmentalists warn of overgrazing, water depletion, and habitat loss (think sage grouse), though hemp and grasses mitigate some strain. Feds counter that these lands belong to all Americans, not just Nevadans. A homestead push would test that balance. Looking Ahead Nevada’s BLM lands aren’t Nebraska’s loamy fields, but they’re not barren either. Hemp farming, grass-fed ranching, and mining could homestead 24–33 million acres, blending economic punch with desert reality. It’s no 1867 redo—water and will limit scale—but a tailored fix for a state long sidelined by its own terrain. As Utah’s legal saga unfolds, Nevada might seize this moment, proving arid lands can yield more than dust and dreams. Congress, take note: the Silver State’s next chapter could rewrite the West’s federal legacy.

text: Below is a draft of proposed legislation titled the Judicial Injunction Reform Act of 2025. This legislation limits district court injunctions to the parties before the court and the judicial district where the court resides by default, with a process for proposing broader orders subject to expedited circuit court review. The draft is written in a formal, legal style consistent with U.S. congressional legislation, drawing on the constitutional authority of Congress under Article III, Section 1 and 2, and the Rules Enabling Act (28 U.S.C. § 2072). It includes a sunset clause for evaluation and avoids direct amendments to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (FRCP) to respect Supreme Court authority while leveraging Congress’s structural powers. 117th Congress, 2nd Session H.R. [Insert Number] Judicial Injunction Reform Act of 2025 AN ACT To limit the scope of injunctions issued by United States district courts, establish a process for review of proposed broader injunctions by circuit courts, and for other purposes. Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE This Act may be cited as the “Judicial Injunction Reform Act of 2025.” SECTION 2. FINDINGS AND PURPOSE (a) Findings—Congress finds the following: Article III of the Constitution of the United States vests Congress with the authority to ordain and establish inferior courts and to make exceptions and regulations to their jurisdiction. Nationwide injunctions issued by United States district courts have, in recent years, disrupted the uniform application of federal laws and policies, often affecting nonparties and jurisdictions beyond the issuing court’s district. Such injunctions have raised concerns about judicial overreach, inconsistent rulings, and the potential for forum shopping, undermining public confidence in the federal judiciary and the balance of powers among the branches of government. A balanced approach is necessary to limit the scope of district court injunctions while preserving judicial discretion in appropriate cases and ensuring higher judicial oversight for broader relief. (b) Purpose—The purpose of this Act is to: Ensure that injunctions issued by United States district courts are, by default, limited to the parties before the court and the judicial district where the court resides. Establish a process for district courts to propose broader injunctions, subject to expedited review and approval by the appropriate United States circuit court of appeals. Promote uniformity, judicial restraint, and respect for the separation of powers under the Constitution. SECTION 3. LIMITATION ON SCOPE OF DISTRICT COURT INJUNCTIONS (a) Default Scope—Except as provided in subsection (b), any preliminary or permanent injunction issued by a United States district court shall: Apply only to the parties named in the action before the court; and Have effect only within the judicial district in which the issuing court resides. (b) Proposed Broader Injunctions— Proposal by District Court—If a United States district court determines that an injunction broader than the scope described in subsection (a) is necessary to prevent irreparable harm, protect constitutional rights, or enforce federal law, the court may issue a proposed order specifying: (A) The geographic scope of the proposed injunction (e.g., circuit-wide, nationwide, or other specified jurisdiction); (B) The legal and factual basis for the broader scope, including the nature and extent of the harm to be prevented, the likelihood of success on the merits, and the public interest; (C) The rationale for extending relief beyond the parties and district, with a clear explanation of why such relief is narrowly tailored to the circumstances. Automatic Referral to Circuit Court—Upon issuance of a proposed broader injunction under paragraph (1), the district court shall immediately refer the proposed order, along with the record of the case, to a three-judge panel of the United States court of appeals for the circuit in which the district court is located. Expedited Review by Circuit Court— (A) The circuit court panel shall review the proposed broader injunction within 14 calendar days of referral, unless extended for good cause shown. (B) The review shall be conducted on an expedited basis, without oral argument unless ordered by the panel, and shall consider: (i) Whether the proposed broader injunction is justified by clear and convincing evidence of irreparable harm, a likelihood of success on the merits, and the public interest; (ii) Whether the scope of the proposed injunction is narrowly tailored to address the specific harm identified; (iii) Whether the proposed injunction complies with applicable constitutional and statutory standards, including the principles of judicial restraint and separation of powers. (C) The circuit court may approve, modify, or reject the proposed broader injunction, issuing a final order with written findings of fact and conclusions of law. Effect of Circuit Court Decision—The district court’s proposed broader injunction shall have no effect until approved or modified by the circuit court. If the circuit court rejects the proposed broader injunction, the district court’s injunction shall revert to the scope described in subsection (a). (c) Applicability—This section applies to all civil actions seeking preliminary or permanent injunctive relief in United States district courts, including but not limited to actions challenging federal statutes, regulations, or executive actions. SECTION 4. PROCEDURAL REQUIREMENTS (a) Notice and Briefing—In any action where a district court considers issuing a proposed broader injunction under section 3(b), the court shall: Provide notice to all parties and, where applicable, the United States Attorney General, of its intent to propose a broader injunction; Allow the parties and the Attorney General, if applicable, to submit briefs addressing the necessity and scope of the proposed broader injunction within 7 days, unless extended for good cause. (b) Reporting Requirement—Each United States district court shall submit an annual report to the Administrative Office of the United States Courts, detailing the number and nature of injunctions issued under this Act, including any proposed broader injunctions referred to circuit courts. SECTION 5. SUNSET PROVISION This Act shall terminate on December 31, 2030, unless reauthorized by Congress. Prior to termination, the Judicial Conference of the United States shall submit a report to Congress evaluating the impact of this Act on judicial efficiency, uniformity, and the balance of powers, including recommendations for permanent legislation or amendments. SECTION 6. CONFORMING AMENDMENTS No amendments to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure or other rules of court practice are required to implement this Act. This Act shall be construed as an exercise of Congress’s authority under Article III of the Constitution to regulate the jurisdiction and procedures of inferior courts. SECTION 7. SEVERABILITY If any provision of this Act, or the application of such provision to any person or circumstance, is held invalid, the remainder of the Act, and the application of such provision to other persons or circumstances, shall not be affected. SECTION 8. EFFECTIVE DATE This Act shall take effect 90 days after the date of its enactment and shall apply to all injunctions issued or proposed after that date. Notes on the Draft Constitutional Authority: The legislation relies on Article III, Sections 1 and 2, which give Congress the power to establish and regulate inferior courts and their jurisdiction. It avoids direct conflict with the FRCP by focusing on statutory limits rather than rule amendments, respecting Supreme Court authority under the Rules Enabling Act. Balancing Act: The default limitation to parties and districts addresses conservative concerns about nationwide injunctions (as in the X post), while the circuit review process ensures judicial discretion and flexibility in rare cases, appealing to moderates and liberals. Political Feasibility: The sunset clause (Section 5) allows for evaluation and adjustment, increasing its chances of passage by addressing potential opposition from judicial or political quarters. The reporting requirement (Section 4(b)) provides transparency and data for future refinement. Practical Implementation: The 14-day circuit review timeline and 7-day briefing period balance efficiency with due process, minimizing delays while ensuring thorough review. The three-judge panel requirement mirrors existing appellate practices, ensuring consistency and expertise.

text: Congress originally got paid per diem—$6 for each day they attended a session, starting in 1789, which would be about $218 a day in today’s money. That changed in 1816 when they switched to a $1,500 annual salary, but public outrage forced them back to per diem until 1855, when salaries became permanent. So, the per diem system lasted from 1789 to 1816, briefly returned after 1816, and was fully replaced by annual salaries in 1855.

text: Singer "P!nk" gets fact checked after posting a fake list of "banned books in Florida." The entertainer has jumped headlong into a nuanced policy discussion ahead of her scheduled tour, and says she'll be distributing the following four book titles during her Florida concert. Ironically, two of the book titles to be handed out are missing from her fake list, while the other two books are not banned in any Florida districts. Let's take a look: "Beloved" by Toni Morrison - Pulitzer Prize-winning 1987 novel about the horrors, positives, and legacy of slavery is "banned" from nine Florida school districts as it depicts the confusing relationship between master and slave in an almost permissible way. "The Family Book" by Todd Parr - a young children's picture book about different families, including same-sex parents. Three districts have added this to their review list, but the book is far from "banned." "The Hill We Climb" by Amanda Gorman - the poem written for President Joe Biden's inauguration - was moved from the elementary library to the middle school section in a Miami school... NOT BANNED "Girls Who Code" by Reshma Saujani was reportedly temporarily removed by a district in Pennsylvania last year but doesn't appear on Pen America's current list. NOT BANNED IN FL. In addition, it should be noted that the state does not ban books. The issue referenced as "book banning" is actually a conversation of age-appropriate teaching materials in K-12 public schools, which are determined at the district level between each school board and the communities they serve. These guidelines are loosely created by state standards, but it ultimately falls to the teachers and parents in each district to determine which instructional materials will be used. The process and guidelines can be found here at the Florida Department of Education- https://fldoe.org/academics/stan dards/instructional-materials/instructional-materials-statutes.stml …

text: Herd Dynamics are so cool! This chestnut mare "Reba" is my lead/alpha cow horse. About every 30 minutes, she'll move 5 feet or so, circling this black cow that's in labor. Now, you'll see this bay mare to the right, watching the woods. She's our other cow horse and hasn't moved in hours. These two girls, who work as a pair here on the farm and in team roping, are keeping watch while also teaching this young paint mare in the very back. You'll also notice our other pregnant cow beside the momma-to-be, keeping her company licking her side and nuzzling her gently. Reminiscent of the "red tent," where women used to care for one another through cycles and births, herds have similar structures up until it's time to push. Once the baby starts to come, momma will break off from the herd and find somewhere dark and quiet. It varies by herd, but on our farm, our cow horses will stand guard outside of the barn until momma and calf emerge. This is why we turn out our cow horses with our bred cows. Many might disagree with me, but in my experience, it causes less injuries as these mommas learn to trust our horses with their calves, and are less likely to try and gore them come spring when we've got to rope, tag, de-horn, castrate, and worm their babies.

text: Recovery and Mental Health I’ve had my fair share of struggles with depression, anxiety, and burnout, and I’ve learned that self-care has to be more than just a buzzword. It has to be something intentional, something that meets you where you’re at. For me, one of the most important steps was seeing a psychiatrist for my medication. It made a big difference to work with someone who really understands mental health meds. I take them every day, same time, just like brushing my teeth. It’s part of my routine now, and that consistency helps keep me grounded. Therapy is a big part of my self-care too. I go every other week and do it virtually, which makes it easier and more comfortable. There’s something about being in your own space that makes it feel safer to process heavy things. I also do things that nurture my body, like getting a massage every three weeks. It helps release the stress I carry physically. And at least twice a month, I give myself a full “do nothing” day; no obligations, no expectations. I shut off my phone and binge-watch light, comforting shows or scroll through TikTok (after tweaking the algorithm to make it less emotionally draining). It’s not lazy. It’s recovery. A happy light has also been helpful, especially during those gloomy days that seem to drag on forever. They’re easy to find online and can really boost your mood if you’re sensitive to the dark. Connection matters too. I check in with my core people and talk openly about what’s going on in my life. Just saying things out loud can lift some of the weight. I refuse to suffer in silence anymore, but I also realize that it’s not fair to make other people responsible for my problems. I try to maintain a few feel-good routines too, like getting my hair done every few months. It’s not about vanity; it’s about feeling human and cared for. I’ve also learned to say “no” when I don’t have the mental space. Boundaries are self-care, and they matter.

text: It’s astonishing that some, like this woman, remain unaware of the deeper issues at play. Allow me to clarify my understanding for those who may not be fully informed: In states like California, Democrats have strategically used illegal immigration to consolidate power. The census counts all residents, including illegal immigrants, and by directing their placement, Democrats can reshape electoral districts to marginalize opposition, making elections predictable. Minnesota serves as a textbook example. Democrats facilitated the resettlement of a large population into a once-competitive region—a battleground of Republicans and Democratic farmers—transforming it into a deep-blue stronghold. This shift is evident in the election of a Somali representative to Congress. What was once a quintessential Midwestern city of blue-collar workers has become “Little Mogadishu,” marked by rising crime, strained resources, and a departure from traditional American values and assimilation. Native residents feel displaced, and the city is unrecognizable to Americans. Democrats want to scale this strategy nationally. By allowing millions of illegal immigrants to cross open borders, Democrats are laying the groundwork for the next phase: securing asylum cases. This is why they oppose deportations and advocate for individuals like Abrego Garcia. Winning these cases sets a precedent to halt deportations broadly, paving the way for amnesty and, ultimately, voting rights. The long-term goal is clear: alter America’s demographic makeup to create a permanent Democratic majority. This approach prioritizes power over the well-being of communities, compromising living standards, safety, and national identity. The endgame is a deep-blue, progressive nation where elections are mere formalities, with outcomes predetermined by a reliant voting bloc. This isn’t just about policy—it’s about fundamentally reshaping America to entrench one-party dominance, regardless of the cost to your family, community, or country.

text: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us, and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom and the power, and the glory, forever and ever. Help us Father to keep your commandments, that we shall not have no other gods before You, that we do not make for ourselves any carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, That we do not take your name (Elohim and Yahweh and El Shaddai and Adonai) in vain, that we keep your 7th day holy, that we honor our fathers and mothers, that we murder not, that we commit adultery not, that we steal not, that we do not bear false witness on our neighbors, help us that we not covet our neighbor's house or shall not covet our neighbor's wife, nor his any person servant of my neighbor's house, nor anything that is our neighbor's. text: Who is John Galt? Some Grok fun comparing the character to @elonmusk You’re drawing a parallel between John Galt and Elon Musk, and it’s not hard to see why some might make that comparison. Musk, like Galt, is a figure who thrives on innovation and sheer force of will—pushing boundaries with companies like Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI, often in defiance of conventional wisdom or bureaucratic resistance. Both are visionaries who prioritize individual initiative and problem-solving over reliance on collectives or established systems. Galt’s fictional strike of the "men of the mind" echoes Musk’s real-world tendency to bypass traditional industries—think of how he’s disrupted automotive giants with electric vehicles or challenged government-dominated space exploration with reusable rockets. Musk’s relentless drive to create, even when faced with skepticism or regulatory pushback, mirrors Galt’s refusal to let a decaying world dictate his terms. And Galt’s hidden utopia, Galt’s Gulch, could be loosely likened to Musk’s ambitious plans, like colonizing Mars as a new frontier for human potential. That said, the analogy isn’t perfect. Galt is an idealized, almost mythic figure—uncompromising, detached, and singularly focused on his principles. Musk, for all his brilliance, is messier: a public persona with quirks, tweets, and a knack for stirring both admiration and controversy. Galt rejects society outright; Musk engages with it, shapes it, and sometimes clashes with it head-on. Where Galt preaches self-interest in a philosophical vacuum, Musk’s ventures—like sustainable energy or neural interfaces—suggest a mix of personal ambition and a broader aim to fix systemic problems. Still, the comparison holds a kernel of truth: both embody a belief that human progress hinges on bold, independent thinkers who don’t wait for permission. Whether Musk would see himself in Galt’s shoes is another question—he’s too busy building rockets to give a radio speech about it.

text: The AR-15 was not created as a sporting rifle. Its origins lie in military design. Eugene Stoner developed the platform in the 1950s with select-fire capability as a fundamental feature. text: One crisp winter morning in Sweden, a cute little girl named Greta woke up to a perfect world, one where there were no petroleum products ruining the earth. She tossed aside her cotton sheet and wool blanket and stepped out onto a dirt floor covered with willow bark that had been pulverized with rocks. “What’s this?” she asked. “Pulverized willow bark,” replied her fairy godmother. “What happened to the carpet?” she asked. “The carpet was nylon, which is made from butadiene and hydrogen cyanide, both made from petroleum,” came the response. Greta smiled, acknowledging that adjustments are necessary to save the planet, and moved to the sink to brush her teeth where instead of a toothbrush, she found a willow, mangled on one end to expose wood fibre bristles. “Your old toothbrush?” noted her godmother, “Also nylon.” “Where’s the water?” asked Greta. “Down the road in the canal,” replied her godmother, ‘Just make sure you avoid water with cholera in it” “Why’s there no running water?” Greta asked, becoming a little peevish. “Well,” said her godmother, who happened to teach engineering at MIT, “Where do we begin?” There followed a long monologue about how sink valves need elastomer seats and how copper pipes contain copper, which has to be mined and how it’s impossible to make all-electric earth-moving equipment with no gear lubrication or tires and how ore has to be smelted to a make metal, and that’s tough to do with only electricity as a source of heat, and even if you use only electricity, the wires need insulation, which is petroleum-based, and though most of Sweden’s energy is produced in an environmentally friendly way because of hydro and nuclear, if you do a mass and energy balance around the whole system, you still need lots of petroleum products like lubricants and nylon and rubber for tires and asphalt for filling potholes and wax and iPhone plastic and elastic to hold your underwear up while operating a copper smelting furnace and . . . “What’s for breakfast?” interjected Greta, whose head was hurting. "Fresh, range-fed chicken eggs,” replied her godmother. “Raw.” “How so, raw?” inquired Greta. “Well, . . .” And once again, Greta was told about the need for petroleum products like transformer oil and scores of petroleum products essential for producing metals for frying pans and in the end was educated about how you can’t have a petroleum-free world and then cook eggs. Unless you rip your front fence up and start a fire and carefully cook your egg in an orange peel like you do in Boy Scouts. Not that you can find oranges in Sweden anymore. “But I want poached eggs like my Aunt Tilda makes,” lamented Greta. “Tilda died this morning,” the godmother explained. “Bacterial pneumonia.” “What?!” interjected Greta. “No one dies of bacterial pneumonia! We have penicillin.” “Not anymore,” explained godmother “The production of penicillin requires chemical extraction using isobutyl acetate, which, if you know your organic chemistry, is petroleum-based. Lots of people are dying, which is problematic because there’s not any easy way of disposing of the bodies since backhoes need hydraulic oil and crematoriums can’t really burn many bodies using as fuel Swedish fences and furniture, which are rapidly disappearing - being used on the black market for roasting eggs and staying warm.” This represents only a fraction of Greta’s day, a day without microphones to exclaim into and a day without much food, and a day without carbon-fibre boats to sail in, but a day that will save the planet. Tune in tomorrow when Greta needs a root canal and learns how Novocain is synthesized.

Unless you rip your front fence up and start a fire and carefully cook your egg in an orange peel like you do in Boy Scouts. Not that you can find oranges in Sweden anymore. “But I want poached eggs like my Aunt Tilda makes,” lamented Greta. “Tilda died this morning,” the godmother explained. “Bacterial pneumonia.” “What?!” interjected Greta. “No one dies of bacterial pneumonia! We have penicillin.” “Not anymore,” explained godmother “The production of penicillin requires chemical extraction using isobutyl acetate, which, if you know your organic chemistry, is petroleum-based. Lots of people are dying, which is problematic because there’s not any easy way of disposing of the bodies since backhoes need hydraulic oil and crematoriums can’t really burn many bodies using as fuel Swedish fences and furniture, which are rapidly disappearing - being used on the black market for roasting eggs and staying warm.” This represents only a fraction of Greta’s day, a day without microphones to exclaim into and a day without much food, and a day without carbon-fibre boats to sail in, but a day that will save the planet. Tune in tomorrow when Greta needs a root canal and learns how Novocain is synthesized.

text: #factcheck: American Tourist’s Wombat Blunder – Misinformation & A Dash of Outrage Breaking: Yet another influencer visits Australia, does something ridiculous, then gets offended when we’re not impressed. This time, it’s @SamanthaStrable (aka Sam Jones), who thought pulling a baby wombat out of its burrow was a solid content strategy. Spoiler: It wasn’t. The Great Wombat Heist Samantha decided to yoink a baby wombat from its mother for a social media video. Because nothing screams “respect for nature” like disturbing a wild animal for clicks. Naturally, Australians reacted as expected—with a mix of outrage, sarcasm, and suggestions that she try the same with a crocodile. Even @AlboMP (Anthony Albanese) weighed in, calling her actions an “outrage” and suggesting she grab a baby croc next time. Tbh, we’d all watch that livestream. Misinformation & The Interview Dodge After realising she’d triggered an entire continent, Samantha issued an apology… kinda. She: Blamed the Australian Government for culling laws. Claimed hypocrisy, comparing controlled population management to her random wombat heist. Tried to justify her actions while completely missing the point. #factcheck: Yes, wildlife management exists in Australia—because unchecked populations can damage ecosystems. No, that’s not the same as random tourists kidnapping baby wombats like they’re plush toys at a gift shop. Wombats have very protective mothers & can easily die from stress. This stunt could have seriously harmed the baby. When @TheProjectTV invited her on for an interview, she bailed at the last minute, opting for a pre-recorded video instead. Host Hamish called her actions “pathetic” & “lousy”—which is pretty much the official Aussie rating for bad excuses. Australia’s Open Invitation for Influencer Chaos Let’s face it, Australia has a long history of influencers coming here, doing something dumb, then fleeing when they get called out. From @LoganPaul filming sacred sites to tourists licking cane toads, there’s a clear pattern of not Googling ‘should I touch this?’ before doing it. But at least they didn’t steal a baby wombat. Moral of the Story: If you’re visiting Australia, respect the wildlife. If you mess up, own it properly. And for the love of wombats, leave baby animals alone. That’s all for today’s #factcheck. text: #FactCheck: Islam, Muslims & Extremists – Stop the Misinformation In the age of rapid information (and misinformation), it’s easy to see how societies like the #UK, #Australia, & #USA struggle to differentiate between #Islam as a religion, everyday #Muslims who practice peacefully, & the #Extremists who make headlines for all the wrong reasons. The result? Fear, suspicion, & unnecessary division. Let’s break it down. ⸻ Islam: A Religion of Over a Billion People #Islam is one of the world’s major religions, practiced by over 1.9 billion people. Like #Christianity & #Judaism, it has a wide range of interpretations, cultural expressions, & levels of observance. At its core, Islam teaches peace, charity, & moral discipline. Most of what #NonMuslims know about #IslamicFaith comes from biased media narratives or cherry-picked Quran verses taken out of context. If you judged #Christianity purely by the actions of the KKK, the Westboro Baptist Church, or the Crusaders, would that be a fair representation? No. So why do it with Islam? ⸻ Muslims: Everyday People Just Living Their Lives #Muslims are people who follow #Islam, just like #Christians follow #Christianity. The majority of Muslims just want to live their lives—work, raise families, build careers & contribute to their communities. Muslims in #WesternCountries are not a monolithic group: Some pray 5 times a day. Some are more culturally Muslim. Some don’t practice at all—just like #CulturalChristians at Christmas. The problem? #Islamophobia. People lump all #Muslims into one category, failing to separate the peaceful majority from the extremists who distort the faith for their own agendas. ⸻ Extremists: A Tiny Minority Hijacking Islam Yes, #IslamicExtremism exists. Groups like #ISIS & #AlQaeda have weaponized #Islam, using selective interpretations to justify violence. But let’s be clear: These groups DO NOT represent Islam. They make up a tiny fraction of the global Muslim population. They kill more Muslims than they do non-Muslims. If Islam inherently promoted terrorism, why would these groups target their own people? The reality is, #Terrorism is about power, control & political agendas—not religion itself. To put it into perspective, #ExtremistMuslims are to Islam what #WhiteSupremacists are to Christianity—dangerous, radical & not representative of the faith. ⸻ The West’s Fear & Misinformation Western societies have a complicated relationship with #Islam, shaped by: • #MediaManipulation • #Fearmongering • #PoliticalRhetoric When a terrorist attack is carried out by a Muslim, it’s blamed on Islam. When a mass shooting happens by a white nationalist, it’s treated as an isolated incident. Some common fears & misconceptions: “They’re taking over!” FACT: Muslims make up only 3.2% of Australia, 6.5% of the UK, & 1.1% of the US. Hardly a takeover. “They don’t assimilate!” FACT: Most #MuslimsInTheWest integrate just fine. They work, pay taxes, & follow the law—just like everyone else. “Sharia Law is coming!” FACT: #ShariaLaw in the West is mostly personal—marriage, dietary laws, etc. The idea that #Australia, #UK, or #America is about to be ruled by Sharia is pure paranoia. ⸻ A More Nuanced Approach Western societies must move past fear & misinformation: Differentiate between #Islam, #Muslims & #Extremists—they are NOT the same thing. Talk to real #Muslims, not just get your info from #MainstreamMedia. Call out #Extremists without blaming 1.9 billion people. ⸻ Final Thoughts #Fear thrives in ignorance. The only way to overcome it is through knowledge. Islam, like any other religion, has good & bad elements. Most #Muslims are just normal people trying to get through life. #Extremists are a dangerous minority, not a representation of Islam. If someone judges an entire faith based on the actions of a few, the problem isn’t the religion—it’s ignorance.
